exercises.prompt: Implement safeDivide(a, b) so it returns a / b, EXCEPT that when b is 0 it throws a RangeError instead of returning Infinity or NaN. safeDivide(6, 2) is 3. safeDivide(1, 0) throws a RangeError. Only a zero divisor is an error — a zero numerator like safeDivide(0, 5) is fine and returns 0.
hints: Guard the bad case first: check the divisor before you divide, and throw when it is 0.
throw new RangeError('...') stops the function with an error; put it inside if (b === 0), and let return a / b sit below it for every valid case.
if (b === 0) throw new RangeError('cannot divide by zero'); return a / b — testing only b (not a) means safeDivide(0, 5) still returns 0, while safeDivide(1, 0) throws.

exercises.prompt: Implement checkedSqrt(x) so it returns the square root of x, but throws a RangeError when x is negative (a real square root is undefined there). checkedSqrt(9) is 3. checkedSqrt(0) is 0. checkedSqrt(-1) throws a RangeError. Use Math.sqrt for the valid case.
hints: Only negative inputs are the problem — zero and positives all have a valid square root.
Check if (x < 0) and throw a RangeError there; otherwise return Math.sqrt(x).
if (x < 0) throw new RangeError('...'); return Math.sqrt(x) — the guard is x < 0, not x <= 0, so checkedSqrt(0) correctly returns 0 instead of throwing.

exercises.prompt: Implement getAt(arr, i) so it returns the element arr[i], but throws a RangeError when i is out of bounds — that is, when i is negative or i is greater than or equal to arr.length. getAt([10, 20, 30], 0) is 10. getAt([10, 20, 30], 3) throws a RangeError, and so does getAt([], 0). Any valid in-range index returns its element.
hints: A valid index runs from 0 up to arr.length − 1; anything outside that — negative, or too big — is an error.
Combine both bad cases in one guard: if (i < 0 || i >= arr.length) throw a RangeError.

if (i < 0 || i >= arr.length) throw new RangeError('index out of range'); return arr[i] — using >= length catches i equal to the length (index 3 on a length-3 array), where plain arr[i] would silently return undefined.

exercises.prompt: Implement parsePositive(n) so it returns n when n is a positive number, but throws a TypeError when n is 0 or negative. parsePositive(5) is 5. parsePositive(0) throws a TypeError, and parsePositive(-3) throws a TypeError. Note the error type here is TypeError, not RangeError.
hints: Positive means strictly greater than 0, so 0 itself is not positive and must be rejected.
Guard with if (n <= 0) and throw new TypeError there — the constructor you choose sets the error's name, which the tests check.
if (n <= 0) throw new TypeError('expected a positive number'); return n — throwing a RangeError instead would fail, because the test asks specifically for a TypeError.

exercises.prompt: Implement withdraw(balance, amount) so it returns the balance remaining after taking amount out — balance − amount — but throws a RangeError for an invalid withdrawal: when amount is negative, or when amount is greater than balance (an overdraft). withdraw(100, 30) is 70. Withdrawing the exact balance is allowed: withdraw(50, 50) is 0. withdraw(100, 150) throws a RangeError, and so does withdraw(100, -5).
hints: Two things make a withdrawal invalid: a negative amount, or an amount larger than the balance — either one should throw.
Combine them: if (amount < 0 || amount > balance) throw a RangeError; otherwise return balance − amount.

if (amount < 0 || amount > balance) throw new RangeError('invalid withdrawal'); return balance - amount — the test is amount > balance, not >=, so withdrawing the exact balance (50 from 50) returns 0 rather than throwing.
